questions.q: The rate equation for a reaction is \(\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^{2}[\mathrm{B}]\), with the rate in \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}\). What are the units of \(k\)?
questions.solution: \(k = \frac{\text{rate}}{[\mathrm{A}]^{2}[\mathrm{B}]}\), with units \(\frac{\text{mol dm}^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}}{(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^{3}} = \text{mol}^{-2}\ \text{dm}^{6}\ \text{s}^{-1}\) for a third-order reaction. (Inverting the concentration units is the common slip.)

questions.q: Initial rates were measured for the reaction of A with B. Experiment 1: \([\mathrm{A}] = 0.10\), \([\mathrm{B}] = 0.20\), initial rate \(4.0 \times 10^{-4}\). Experiment 2: \([\mathrm{A}] = 0.20\), \([\mathrm{B}] = 0.20\), initial rate \(1.6 \times 10^{-3}\). Experiment 3: \([\mathrm{A}] = 0.10\), \([\mathrm{B}] = 0.60\), initial rate \(1.2 \times 10^{-3}\). (Concentrations in \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\); rates in \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}\).) What is the rate equation?
questions.solution: Experiments 1 and 2: \([\mathrm{A}]\) doubles, \([\mathrm{B}]\) is constant, and the rate goes up 4 times, so the reaction is second order in A. Experiments 1 and 3: \([\mathrm{B}]\) triples and the rate triples, so it is first order in B. Rate \(= k[\mathrm{A}]^{2}[\mathrm{B}]\). (Reading the threefold rise in experiment 3 as third order in B is the common slip.)

questions.q: For the reaction of A with B, \(\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^{2}[\mathrm{B}]\). When \([\mathrm{A}] = 0.10\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) and \([\mathrm{B}] = 0.20\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\), the initial rate is \(4.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}\). What is the value of \(k\), in \(\text{mol}^{-2}\ \text{dm}^{6}\ \text{s}^{-1}\)?
A reaction is zero order with respect to reactant X. What happens to the rate when the concentration of X is tripled, with everything else unchanged?
questions.solution: Zero order means \(\text{rate} \propto [\mathrm{X}]^{0} = 1\): the concentration of X does not affect the rate at all. (Tripling would be first order and nine times second order.)

questions.q: The graph shows how the initial rate of a reaction depends on the concentration of reactant Q. What is the order of reaction with respect to Q?

figure.alt: Initial rate against concentration of Q: a curve through the origin that gets steeper. At 0.20 mol per dm cubed the rate is 0.6; at 0.40 it is 2.4 (units of 10 to the minus 4 mol per dm cubed per second).

questions.solution: When \([\mathrm{Q}]\) doubles from 0.20 to 0.40, the rate goes from 0.6 to 2.4, four times larger: \(2^{n} = 4\), so \(n = 2\). The rising, curving line through the origin is the shape for second order. (A curve that bends upward is not first order: first order gives a straight line through the origin.)

questions.q: The graph shows how the concentration of reactant X changes during a reaction that is zero order with respect to X. What is the rate constant?

figure.alt: Concentration of X against time: a straight line falling from 0.080 mol per dm cubed at 0 minutes to 0.020 mol per dm cubed at 5 minutes.

questions.solution: For zero order, rate \(= k\), and the rate is the gradient's size. The concentration falls by \(0.080 - 0.020 = 0.060\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) in 5 minutes \(= 300\ \text{s}\). So \(k = \frac{0.060}{300} = 2.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}\). (Leaving the time in minutes leads to \(1.2 \times 10^{-2}\).)

questions.q: In a first-order reaction, the concentration of the reactant falls from \(0.64\) to \(0.08\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) in 90 s. Use \(k = \frac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}}\) to find the rate constant.
questions.solution: 0.64 to 0.32 to 0.16 to 0.08 is three half-lives, so \(t_{1/2} = 90 \div 3 = 30\ \text{s}\). Then \(k = \frac{\ln 2}{30} = 0.0231\ \text{s}^{-1}\). (Taking 90 s as one half-life leads to 0.00770.)

questions.q: Which feature of a concentration–time graph shows that a reaction is first order with respect to the reactant?

options.B: The graph is a straight line with a negative gradient.
options.C: Each half-life is twice as long as the one before.
options.D: The concentration reaches zero after two half-lives.

questions.solution: For a first-order reaction the half-life does not depend on the concentration, so successive half-lives are constant. A straight line is zero order, and half-lives that lengthen as the concentration falls are second order. (Confusing the straight line of zero order with first order is the common slip.)

questions.q: For \(\mathrm{2NO_{2}(g) + F_{2}(g) \rightarrow 2NO_{2}F(g)}\), the rate equation is \(\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{NO_{2}}][\mathrm{F_{2}}]\). Which mechanism is consistent with this?

options.B: Step 1 (fast): \(\mathrm{NO_{2} + F_{2} \rightarrow NO_{2}F + F}\); step 2 (slow): \(\mathrm{NO_{2} + F \rightarrow NO_{2}F}\)
options.C: Step 1 (slow): \(\mathrm{NO_{2} + F_{2} \rightarrow NO_{2}F + F}\); step 2 (fast): \(\mathrm{NO_{2} + F \rightarrow NO_{2}F}\)

questions.solution: The rate equation shows one \(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\) and one \(\mathrm{F_{2}}\) take part in the rate-determining step, so the slow step must be \(\mathrm{NO_{2} + F_{2} \rightarrow NO_{2}F + F}\). The second \(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\) reacts afterwards, in a fast step. A single step would make it second order in \(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\). (Taking the overall equation as the slow step is the common slip.)

questions.q: The hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane by hydroxide ions has the rate equation \(\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{(CH_{3})_{3}CBr}]\). What does this show about the mechanism?

options.A: Hydroxide ions are in the rate-determining step, so the mechanism is SN2.
options.B: Hydroxide ions act as a catalyst.
options.C: The reaction happens in a single step involving both reactants.
options.D: Only the halogenoalkane is in the rate-determining step, so the mechanism is SN1.

questions.solution: Zero order in \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) means the hydroxide ion is not in the slow step. The slow step is the halogenoalkane breaking to a carbocation and a bromide ion, which the hydroxide ion then attacks in a fast step: SN1, unimolecular. (Assuming every reactant appears in the rate equation is the common slip.)

questions.q: The acid-catalysed reaction of propanone with iodine has the rate equation \(\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{CH_{3}COCH_{3}}][\mathrm{H^{+}}]\). Which statement is correct?

options.A: Iodine reacts in a fast step after the rate-determining step.
options.C: Iodine reacts in the rate-determining step.
options.D: The reaction can happen without iodine.

questions.solution: Zero order in iodine means iodine is not in the rate-determining step or any step before it; it reacts in a later, fast step. Propanone and \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) are in the slow step, and \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) is the catalyst, regenerated at the end. (Iodine is a reactant and is used up, so it cannot be the catalyst.)

questions.q: Which statement best explains why the rate constant, \(k\), increases when the temperature is raised?

options.A: The activation energy decreases as the temperature rises.
options.B: The Arrhenius constant, A, increases sharply with temperature.
options.C: A much larger fraction of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy.
options.D: The particles collide more often, and this is the main reason for the increase.

questions.solution: In \(k = A\mathrm{e}^{-E_{\text{a}}/RT}\), raising \(T\) makes \(\mathrm{e}^{-E_{\text{a}}/RT}\), the fraction of collisions with at least \(E_{\text{a}}\), much larger. More frequent collisions add only a little. (The activation energy is fixed for a reaction unless a catalyst is added.)

questions.q: The graph of \(\ln k\) against \(\frac{1}{T}\) for a reaction is a straight line. Using \(\ln k = -\frac{E_{\text{a}}}{RT} + \ln A\), what is the activation energy? (\(R = 8.31\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\))

figure.alt: ln k against 1/T: a straight line falling from ln k = −4.5 at 1/T = 3.0 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹ to ln k = −8.4 at 1/T = 3.6 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹.

questions.solution: Gradient \(= \frac{-8.4 - (-4.5)}{(3.6 - 3.0) \times 10^{-3}} = -6500\ \text{K}\). The gradient is \(-\frac{E_{\text{a}}}{R}\), so \(E_{\text{a}} = 6500 \times 8.31 = 54000\ \text{J mol}^{-1} = 54.0\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). (Ignoring the \(10^{-3}\) on the axis leads to 0.0540.)

questions.q: For a first-order reaction, \(A = 2.0 \times 10^{11}\ \text{s}^{-1}\) and \(E_{\text{a}} = 85\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). Use \(k = A\mathrm{e}^{-E_{\text{a}}/RT}\) to calculate \(k\) at 77 °C. (\(R = 8.31\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\))
questions.solution: \(T = 77 + 273 = 350\ \text{K}\) and \(E_{\text{a}} = 85000\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\). \(\frac{E_{\text{a}}}{RT} = \frac{85000}{8.31 \times 350} = 29.2\), so \(k = 2.0 \times 10^{11} \times \mathrm{e}^{-29.2} = 0.0406\ \text{s}^{-1}\). (Using the temperature in °C leads to \(4.1 \times 10^{-47}\).)

questions.q: Which technique would continuously monitor the rate of the acid-catalysed reaction between propanone and iodine?

options.A: Measuring the absorbance of the mixture with a colorimeter as the iodine colour fades
options.B: Collecting the gas given off in a gas syringe
options.C: Timing how long a fixed amount of iodine takes to be used up, in separate experiments
options.D: Weighing the reaction flask as mass is lost

questions.solution: Iodine is the only coloured species, so its concentration can be followed throughout the reaction by colorimetry: continuous monitoring. No gas forms, so the gas syringe and mass-loss methods cannot work, and timing a fixed amount of reaction is an initial-rate (clock) method. (Calling a clock method continuous monitoring is the common slip.)

questions.q: In an iodine clock experiment, the time, \(t\), taken for the blue-black colour to appear is measured for different starting concentrations. Which quantity is proportional to the initial rate?
questions.solution: The colour appears when a fixed amount of iodine has formed, so the rate is that fixed amount divided by the time: \(\text{rate} \propto \frac{1}{t}\). A faster reaction gives a shorter time. (Taking the time itself as the rate is the common slip.)

questions.q: For a reaction with \(\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]\), which change increases the value of \(k\)?

options.B: Halving the volume of the reaction mixture
options.C: Removing the product as it forms

questions.solution: The rate constant depends on temperature (and on a catalyst), not on concentrations. Changing a concentration changes the rate, but \(k\) stays the same. (Confusing a faster rate with a larger \(k\) is the common slip.)

questions.q: For \(\mathrm{2NO(g) + 2H_{2}(g) \rightarrow N_{2}(g) + 2H_{2}O(g)}\), the rate equation is \(\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{NO}]^{2}[\mathrm{H_{2}}]\). Which statement is correct?

options.A: The orders could have been predicted from the balanced equation.
options.B: The rate-determining step involves two \(\mathrm{H_{2}}\) molecules.
options.C: The reaction is fourth order overall.
options.D: The rate-determining step involves two \(\mathrm{NO}\) and one \(\mathrm{H_{2}}\), or species formed from them.

questions.solution: The orders show what takes part in the rate-determining step (and any steps before it): two \(\mathrm{NO}\) and one \(\mathrm{H_{2}}\). The second \(\mathrm{H_{2}}\) reacts in a later, fast step. The overall order is \(2 + 1 = 3\). (Reading orders from the balanced equation is the common slip: they come only from experiment.)
